title: Statistics
prerequisites: Ability to calculate an average of a set of numbers.
Familiarity with tables and bar graphs.
Basic understanding of fractions and percentages.
Skill in plotting points on a graph.

topics.title: Collection and Presentation of Data
topics.quick_summary: Raw data is organised into frequency distributions and displayed as bar graphs, histograms or frequency polygons to make patterns visible.
topics.real_life: A histogram of a class's marks shows at a glance whether the paper was easy or hard — something a list of eighty numbers never could.

detailed.definition: Primary data is collected by the investigator directly; secondary data is obtained from an existing source. Class size is the difference between the upper and lower limits of a class, and the class mark is their average.
detailed.key_idea: A histogram is not a bar graph. Histogram bars touch because the variable is continuous, whereas bar graph bars are separated because the categories are discrete.
detailed.working_principle: For a grouped frequency distribution with unequal class sizes, the height of each histogram bar must be adjusted so that area, not height, represents frequency.
applications: Discontinuous classes such as 10–19, 20–29 are made continuous by subtracting 0.5 from lower limits and adding 0.5 to upper limits.
A frequency polygon is drawn by joining the mid-points of the tops of histogram bars.

points: Primary data is first-hand; secondary data comes from an existing source.
In a histogram the bars touch; in a bar graph they do not.
With unequal class sizes, the AREA of each bar must be proportional to the frequency.
mistakes: Drawing a histogram with gaps between the bars.
Using raw frequencies as heights when class sizes are unequal.
Forgetting to convert discontinuous classes into continuous ones before drawing.
topics.memory_hook: 'Histogram bars touch, bar-graph bars do not' — continuous versus categorical.
topics.advanced: Choosing the class width is a genuine trade-off: too wide hides structure, too narrow shows noise. Statisticians use rules such as Sturges' formula, but the honest answer is that several widths should be tried.

topics.title: Mean, Median and Mode
topics.quick_summary: The mean is the arithmetic average, the median is the middle value when data is arranged in order, and the mode is the most frequent value.
topics.real_life: Average income in a town is misleading if one billionaire lives there — the median gives a far truer picture of a typical resident.

detailed.definition: Mean = sum of observations ÷ number of observations. Median is the middle observation of ordered data. Mode is the observation occurring most often.
detailed.key_idea: The mean is pulled by extreme values while the median is not. Choosing between them is a judgement about whether outliers are meaningful or distorting.
detailed.working_principle: For n observations arranged in order, the median is the (n+1)/2 th value when n is odd, and the average of the n/2 th and (n/2 + 1)th values when n is even.
applications: The median is preferred for income, house prices and any skewed data.
The mode is the only average usable for non-numerical data such as favourite colour.

points: Mean = Σx / n; for grouped data, mean = Σfx / Σf.
Median: order the data first — this step is essential and often forgotten.
Mode is the most frequent value; a data set may have more than one mode or none.
The mean is affected by extreme values; the median is not.
mistakes: Finding the median without first arranging the data in order.
Using n/2 as the median position for odd n instead of (n+1)/2.
Reporting the frequency instead of the observation as the mode.
topics.memory_hook: 'Mean adds, Median orders, Mode counts' — three different questions about the same data.
topics.advanced: Mean, median and mode coincide in a perfectly symmetric distribution. The size and direction of the gap between them is a standard measure of skewness — which is what the empirical relation is really capturing.

formulas.name: Mean of Grouped Data
formulas.variables: fᵢ = frequency of the ith class, xᵢ = class mark of the ith class.
formulas.common_mistakes: Using the class limits instead of the class marks as xᵢ.
formulas.shortcut: The assumed-mean method reduces arithmetic when the class marks are large.

formulas.name: Median
formulas.formula: n odd: ((n+1)/2)th term;  n even: mean of (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th terms
formulas.variables: n = number of observations, arranged in ascending order.
formulas.when_to_use: When the data contains extreme values that would distort the mean.
formulas.common_mistakes: Failing to sort the data before locating the middle term.
formulas.shortcut: Sort first, always — the formula is meaningless on unsorted data.
